title: Sum-of-squares compilation of matrix-model dynamics for NISQ and fault-tolerant hardware
abstract: The SU$(N)$ matrix-model potential $V=-\tfrac{g^2}{4}\sum_{I,J}Tr[X_I,X_J]^2$, the interaction of the BFSS/BMN family, whose thermal large-$N$ states are dual to black holes, is diagonal in the coordinate basis and is compiled in the literature as a phase polynomial with $O(d^2N^4Q^4)$ rotations per Trotter step. That cost is close to optimal for its gate class: we show that for a generic Trotter step the Walsh support $m_{\min}$ lower-bounds both the rotation count and the two-qubit count of every circuit over $\{CNOT,CZ,CPhase,R_{ZZ},SWAP,X,R_z\}$, ancillas included, and we build a parity network attaining $1.01$--$1.10\,m_{\min}$. Improvement therefore requires a gate outside that class, and the exact factorisation of $V$ into a sum of squared commutator entries supplies one in each era. For NISQ, Hadamard: each squared entry is added into a Fourier register and squared there, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^3)$ two-qubit gates. For fault tolerance, $T$: reversible arithmetic with one phase-gradient injection per squared entry, $Θ(d^2N^3Q^2)$ T gates and no arbitrary-angle rotation. Both are built and verified. With a native $R_{ZZ}$ the NISQ circuit uses fewer two-qubit gates than every parity network from $Q=6$ at SU(2) and $Q=2$ at SU(5); the oracle beats a precision-matched Hamming-weight-phasing incumbent at every point built except the smallest, by up to $11.9\times$ in T count and, at equal width, $25.5\times$ in surface-code spacetime. An ablation with the same arithmetic but no factorisation costs up to $21\times$ more and loses to that incumbent at $15$ of $17$ points, so the factorisation, not the arithmetic, produces the win. Both constructions survive the supersymmetric deformation to mini-BMN with fermions, and complete Trotter evolutions on a statevector simulator reproduce the exact product formula to $2\times10^{-12}$.
summary: This work tackles the quantum simulation of $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model dynamics, crucial for understanding black hole physics. The authors develop highly efficient quantum circuits for both near-term (NISQ) and fault-tolerant hardware. By exploiting the mathematical structure of the potential's factorization, they achieve significant reductions in required quantum gates compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the resource cost of compiling the time evolution generated by a complex $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model potential for quantum computation.
main_result: The authors propose factorizing the potential into a sum of squared commutator entries, leading to significantly reduced gate counts (both two-qubit and T-gate) compared to standard compilation methods.
method: They derive resource bounds using the Walsh support ($m_{\min}$) and construct specific quantum circuits for both NISQ (using Fourier registers) and fault-tolerant (using reversible arithmetic) hardware.
model_or_system: The system is the $	ext{SU}(N)$ matrix-model potential $V = - rac{g^2}{4}\sum_{I,J}	ext{Tr}[X_I,X_J]^2$, derived from the BFSS/BMN family, whose dynamics are relevant to black hole physics.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate count (NISQ), T-gate count (Fault-Tolerant), and comparison against the theoretical lower bound ($m_{\min}$).
important_parameters: The scaling depends on the dimension ($d$), matrix size ($N$), and grid size ($Q$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on compiling the potential term for a single Trotter step, and comparisons are made against specific gate sets and incumbent compilation techniques.
figures_summary: The notes mention tables comparing resource requirements across different hardware regimes and circuit types, showing crossover points where the proposed method outperforms incumbents.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model and the computational challenge, derives theoretical lower bounds, and then presents and verifies two optimized circuit constructions (NISQ and FT) by exploiting the potential's factorization.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, resource-aware quantum circuit implementations for simulating complex, high-dimensional quantum field theories relevant to quantum gravity and condensed matter models.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The NISQ gadget for one squared quantity v. A±: the Fourier addition of ±v/2r, applied through the fold wire F (steps 2 and 5, Fig. 13); the system is in the prefix-difference basis (∆) for the whole potential step. QFTns: QFT without swaps (the bit reversal is absorbed into the level assignment, Remark 2). The square is a quadratic form in the register bits. One fold wire and one w-qubit register serve all gadgets sequentially.

FIG. 2: NISQ, potential term. (a) Two-qubit gates per Trotter step, SU(2), d = 2, adjoint route: the floor mmin of every parity network, the built structure-aware network, ours with native RZZ and with CNOT only (register frames), and the secondary baselines of Appendix C. (b) mmin divided by our count in each gate set (> 1: fewer two-qubit gates than any parity network in that gate set), SU(2) adjoint and the matrix-entry route at N = 3, 4, 5. (c) Two-qubit depth.

(b) Built network divided by ours, on all-to-all hardware (the logical counts), heavy-hex and the 10 × 12 square lattice, for both gate sets. Counts are in Table XV.
